title: Somebody Told the Bees
spine: finding out why every bee in the garden flies past the best flowers to get somewhere else

hero_name.role: the child in the garden who works the mystery out

first_clue.role: the clue the child chose to follow in the garden
first_clue.default: the two fat pockets of yellow on the bee's back legs

segments.text:
{hero_name}'s pink flowers grew in a pot by the back door, and they were the best flowers in the garden. {hero_name} had watered them every morning for a week.
A bee came past {hero_name}'s ear, close enough to move the air.
It did not stop.
Another came, and then three more, and then too many to count. They all came up out of the two white boxes at the bottom of the garden, and they all went the same way. Over the grass. Over the far fence. Gone.
Barnaby watched them go. Barnaby was a very large and very serious old dog, and he went wherever {hero_name} went.
"They ignored us," he said. He took it personally. He took most things personally.
{hero_name} crouched down by the pot. The pink flowers stayed wide open and empty, every single one of them.
"Barnaby," said {hero_name}. "How does every one of those bees know where to go?"

The bee on the lavender was working the way {hero_name} works a bowl of cereal. Head down. No time for talking.
{hero_name} knelt in close.
On each back leg the bee had a fat little pocket of yellow, packed on tight, like butter pressed onto a knife. She shoved into one purple flower and came out yellower. She shoved into the next one and came out yellower still.
"Pollen," said {hero_name}. "Barnaby, look at her legs. She is taking it home."
Barnaby leaned in to see. His nose came so close that the bee walked round to the other side of the flower and carried on.
"Rude," said Barnaby.
Then up she went, over the grass, over the fence, one small bee with her legs full, going exactly where all the others were going.
Every bee knew. Nobody had told {hero_name}.

{hero_name} turned the bucket upside down and stood on it to see over the fence.
The bees had made a road in the air.
Going out, they crossed at the same spot every time, just above the wobbly post. Coming home, they used the air lower down, sliding along over the grass towards the white boxes. Out along the top, back along the bottom, like the two escalators at the shops.
"They are all doing the same thing," said {hero_name}. "Barnaby. Every one of them is doing exactly the same thing."
Barnaby sat down on {hero_name}'s foot, which was how he agreed with things.
One bee came home so low and so heavy that she nearly parted his ears. She lifted at the last moment, landed on the white box, and walked in through the little door.
Whatever they were fetching, it was worth the whole long way.
Every bee knew the road. Nobody had told {hero_name}.

Ada keeps the two white boxes. She was down at the bottom of the garden with her sleeves rolled up, watching the bees come and go.
"Ada," said {hero_name}. "Not one of them will come to my pink flowers."
{hero_name} told her about {first_clue}.
"Good noticing," said Ada. "That is half of it already. Come and stand by me. Still hands, slow feet. Then they go round us the way water goes round a stone."
So {hero_name} stood still beside her. A bee landed on {hero_name}'s wrist, walked two steps, and lifted off again. Barnaby stood still too, and held his breath, just in case.
{hero_name} put an ear near the wood. The box hummed like the fridge at night. In there, in the dark, were thousands of them.
"They are not ignoring your flowers," said Ada. "They found somewhere better. And then somebody told them where it is."
"Told them?" said {hero_name}. "Bees tell each other things?"

Ada slid back a small wooden shutter. Under it was a window of glass, and under the glass was the dark.
{hero_name}'s eyes took a moment. Then the dark filled up with bees, hundreds of them, walking about on a wall of yellow comb. One came in with two yellow pockets on her legs and pushed them off into a hole in the comb.
"Watch this one," whispered Ada.
One bee was doing something nobody else was doing. She walked a short straight line, shaking her back end so fast that it blurred. Then she curved round and walked the very same line again. And again.
The bees near her pressed in and touched her all over with their feelers.
"The straight part tells them which way," said Ada. "A long shake means far. She has been somewhere good, and now the whole house knows."
One by one, the bees who had touched her turned round, went out of the door, and crossed the fence exactly the way she said.
Ada put a drop of honey on {hero_name}'s finger. It tasted of clover.
Barnaby licked the finger clean and did not apologise.

Out at the corner gate, the field on the other side had gone white. Clover. All the way across, more clover than anybody could pick in a week.
{hero_name} stopped to listen. The whole field was humming, low and busy, the way the kitchen sounds through the door when everyone in there is making lunch.
"There it is," said Ada. "It opened on Tuesday. Every hive for a mile knows."
The bees were rolling about in the little white heads and coming out dusty. {hero_name} watched one pat the yellow dust into the pockets on her back legs, fatter, fatter, and then she was up and away home, low over the grass.
Barnaby lay down in the clover and let a bee walk right across his paw without moving one hair, which for Barnaby was an enormous thing to manage.
They followed that bee home. Just inside the little door of the white box, where the light stopped, she walked a short straight line and shook her back end at everyone.
"That is her telling them," said Ada. "Which way. How far."
{hero_name} picked one clover flower for the kitchen table.

choice_points.question: "Two things worth looking at," said Barnaby, pointing his nose. "That one on the lavender, doing something with her legs. Or the whole lot of them, crossing the fence in a line. Legs, or fence?"

options.label: Look close at the one bee on the lavender

sets_slots.first_clue: the two fat pockets of yellow on the bee's back legs

options.label: Follow the line of bees over the fence

sets_slots.first_clue: the road the bees had made in the air over the fence

choice_points.question: "Two ways to find out," said Ada. "There is a little window in the side of this box, and through it you can watch them tell each other. Or we can walk out to the corner and see the place they were told about. Window, or field?"

options.label: Watch them tell each other through the little window
Walk out and see the place they were told about

request.family_context: insects family shelf already holds The Grand Bug Hotel (insects, make_and_build), The Great Puddle Bridge (ants, make_and_build) and The Meadow Behind Grandpa Milo's House (fireflies, quiet_hour)

pattern_choice.why: The waggle dance is the rare piece of real science that is shaped exactly like a mystery answer: it is invisible, it is genuinely surprising, and it explains something a five-year-old can see with their own eyes in a garden. The question comes free and needs no invention, because bees really do stream past good flowers to reach better ones, and clues really do accumulate on the way to the comb: loaded legs, a flight line, a humming box, a dance in the dark. Nothing is at stake and nobody is worried; the fuel is only wanting to know.

candidates.rejected_because: a garden crossed in a minute gives a journey nowhere to go, and the honest alternative, shrinking a child down to travel inside the hive, throws away the best thing this topic has: that the whole mystery is visible from the back step of a real house

two of the three stories already on the insects shelf are make_and_build, so a third would make the family read as one long craft session; and the obvious build, a bee hotel, is a solitary-bee project that has nothing to do with a hive that dances
the fireflies deep dive already holds the quiet remembered evening for this family, and a hive at work is the loudest, most purposeful thing in a garden; the tone would have to fight the topic

tone_choice.accent_carrier: Barnaby, the very large and very serious old dog. Every light beat in the story is his and only his: taking the bees' indifference personally, calling a bee rude, sitting on a foot as a way of agreeing, holding his breath at the hive just in case, licking the honey off a finger without apologising, and holding perfectly still under a walking bee as an act of enormous self-control. The bees, the flowers, the clover field and the dance itself stay in pure wonder with no jokes in them at all.
tone_choice.why: Wonder is what the answer deserves: a message passed in the dark by dancing is astonishing on its own and needs no help. The silly accent has one job, which is to keep the register light around a hive, where a five-year-old might otherwise arrive with somebody else's fear already installed. A solemn dog who is offended by bees is funnier than a bee could ever be, and it means the bees themselves never have to be made cute or made safe.

rejected.recipe: cozy dominant with a curious_wonder accent
rejected.because: that is exactly the recipe of the fireflies story on the same shelf, and cozy would soften the moment of finding out, which wants a jolt rather than a settle

rejected.recipe: silly dominant with a curious_wonder accent
rejected.because: if the whole garden is funny, the dance becomes another joke; the answer has to arrive in a room where nobody is being funny

teller_choice.why: The pleasure of this mystery is watching somebody notice, and a named child the listener has christened is easier to admire for noticing than a we who is partly the listener. It also lets the listening child be a step back from the hive, which suits a real place: they watch a child their own age stand still beside Ada rather than being told to do it themselves. The narrator never addresses the listener at all.

rejected.because: six of the pilots use it and both existing make_and_build stories in this family use it; more importantly, we-in-the-garden turns the competence beat into an instruction aimed at the listener, which is the one thing rule 11 says not to do
a remembered summer puts the clues in the past tense of somebody else's childhood, and a mystery wants the clue to be in front of us right now

value_decision.why: No condition for including a value lesson is met. The materials produced no natural value angle, this is a library story with no parent value picks attached, and there is no interpersonal moment to hang one on. Standing still beside the hive is competence, not virtue, and reading it as good behaviour would turn the one safety beat into a lesson.

cast.why: New. The insects family has never used named_hero, so there was no existing garden child to bring back. Defined by role and given the naming slot, so whatever the listener calls this child can walk into any later bees story.

cast.role: Barnaby, the very serious old dog
cast.why: New, and invented for reuse. This family had no accent carrier that works outdoors in a plain garden; the grasshopper who boings belongs to a bug hotel and the ant scout to a puddle. A dog who follows a child everywhere can be in every garden story this family ever writes, and he is given a fixed name rather than a slot because the story already spends one naming slot on the hero and the choice questions need him to be addressable by name.

cast.role: Ada, who keeps the two white boxes
cast.why: New. A hive needs a grown-up who is unbothered by it, and no existing family character could hold that job: Grandpa Milo is a rememberer inside a frame story, and the parent insects story has no adults in it at all. Registered to the family for reuse in any hive or orchard story.

Considered and deliberately left out, even though reuse across a topic family is the preferred design. Two reasons, both structural: a mystery needs every pair of eyes pointed at the bees, and an inspector whose established job is examining things would take clue-finding away from the hero; and she would be a second comic character in a story whose tone recipe allows exactly one, which the accent rule forbids. She is still available to the bees topic for a later make_and_build story about planting a flower patch.

selected: wonder-fact: a bee tells the rest of the hive where flowers are by dancing on the comb in the dark, walking a short straight run over and over
wonder-fact: the direction of that straight run says which way to fly, and a longer shake means further away
wonder-fact: the watching bees crowd in and touch the dancer with their antennae, then fly out the way she indicated
wonder-fact: bees carry pollen home packed onto their back legs, and push it off into a cell of the comb when they arrive
wonder-fact: a whole colony will pass by nearer flowers to work a big patch that has just come into bloom
sensory picture: the outbound and inbound flight lines crossing a fence at two different heights
sensory picture: a hive humming through the wood like a fridge heard at night
sensory picture: a clover field in bloom, white right across, loud with bees
setting: a small back garden with two white hive boxes at the bottom and a field over the fence
gathered_but_unused: how honey is actually made, nectar carried in the stomach and fanned down thick: true and lovely, but it is a second mechanism and this story already has one to land
the round dance used for flowers very close to the hive: a real refinement of the waggle dance and precisely the thing that would blur the answer at five
queen, workers and drones as one team: the age-9 system treatment for this node, and the age-8 treatment of the parent
bees seeing colours we cannot, and flower markings that work like landing lights: strong candidate for a flowers_and_pollination story
a beekeeper's smoke and veil: cut on purpose, because the gear invites the question of what the gear is for, and that question is the age-5 avoid list
swarming, a hive splitting and hanging in a tree: forbidden by the inherited insects avoid list at this age

branch_design.why_here: One segment in, at the moment the question has just been asked out loud and two clues are lying in plain sight. Both branches are ways of watching the same bees and both end with a bee going in at the little door of the white box, so s3 opens at the hive whichever was chosen, and needs nothing from either branch except a clue to have been found. That clue is carried in the first_clue slot and named back in one line.

criteria.more_interesting: one branch is a single bee an inch from the face, getting visibly yellower flower by flower; the other is the shape of the whole traffic pattern seen from on top of a bucket. Small and close against big and wide.
criteria.more_engaging: kneeling nose to nose with a working bee and climbing on something to see over a fence are both things a five-year-old does without being asked
criteria.reveals_taste: the lavender branch is gentle and patient; standing up on the bucket to see over the fence is bold
criteria.reveals_curiosity: legs is how-it-works, the mechanics of the pockets and how they fill; fence is what-its-for, what the whole line of them is actually accomplishing
criteria.reflects_mood: the lavender branch is still and quiet and asks nothing of the listener; the fence branch has climbing and near-misses and a dog nearly having his ears parted

branch_design.why_here: Right after the answer is spoken and before it is seen, at the only line in the story with real anticipation in it. Splitting here means the child chooses which half of a true answer to receive first, and both halves satisfy: the message being sent, or the place the message is about. Both endings show a bee dancing and both show pollen riding home on legs, so no path leaves without the science.

criteria.more_interesting: s4a is a shutter sliding back on a dark city of comb; s4b is a whole white field roaring quietly on the other side of a gate. Indoors and secret against outdoors and enormous.
criteria.more_engaging: watching the actual telling and going to see the treasure are the two things any listener wants at that moment, and children split cleanly between them
criteria.reveals_taste: the window is gentle, close, whispered; walking out through the gate into the field is bold
criteria.reveals_curiosity: window is how-it-works, the dance decoded line by line; field is just-experience, the sound and the dust and a bee on a paw
criteria.reflects_mood: the window ending is small and quiet and ends on a taste of honey; the field ending has an outdoor walk in it, and lands on a picked flower for the kitchen table

gates.notes: Six segments, two choice points, wired s1 to c1 to s2a or s2b to s3 to c2 to s4a or s4b, both endings next null. c1 rejoins and both its branches converge on s3, which the validator confirms. s3 depends on nothing either branch invented: the hive, Ada and the pink flowers are all established in s1, and the branch-specific clue enters through the first_clue slot. Avoid-list sweep against knowledge_domain.bees age 5 and the inherited knowledge_domain.insects age 5 list: no sting appears in any form, nothing is painful, nobody swats or squashes, there is no swarm and nothing menacing. Say-words legs and fence, window and field: two syllables at most, no shared onset or rhyme inside a pair.

Measured word counts: s1 155, s2a 148, s2b 152, s3 158, s4a 202, s4b 199. The two endings sit above the 170 aim and were re-read line by line for padding; both were cut, and what remains is beat rather than decoration. s4a needs the shutter, the arriving pollen carrier, the dance itself, the antennae, Ada's two-sentence decoding, the bees acting on the message, and the honey landing. s4b needs the field, its sound, the legs filling, and the dance glimpsed at the doorway so the answer lands on this path too. Paths measure 613 words for legs plus window, 664 for legs plus field, 617 for fence plus window and 668 for fence plus field, all near the 600 aim. Every segment carries at least one spoken line. Sentence length alternates in all six: three-word sentences (It did not stop. Head down. Clover.) sit against sentences of thirty. No abstract mood words. Every object introduced is used: the pink flowers open the mystery and are answered in s3, the white boxes are entered in both branches, the bucket is stood on, the honey and the clover flower are what comes home.

All four paths read aloud end to end. The rejoin holds: both branches close on the same two-sentence motif beat and on a bee heading into the hive, so s3 opens at the boxes without a seam, and the first_clue line is grammatical in both readings. The motif runs question to statement to sight on every path: how does every one of them know, nobody had told the hero, somebody told them, that is her telling them. The competence beat happens exactly once per path, in s3, spoken by Ada as positioning rather than caution. Banned-language sweep clean: no assessment, mastery, score, milestone, is or are behind, ahead of, delayed, gifted, grade level. No ellipses, asterisks, parentheses or emojis anywhere; no stage directions. The hero is never addressed by the narrator and never given a pronoun, so any name the child chooses reads correctly.

writers_notes: The hero is written entirely without pronouns. A name the child supplies cannot be assumed to carry he, she or they, so every sentence that needed one was rebuilt around the name instead. This is a constraint any future named_hero story in this family will inherit.
The word sting never appears, and neither does any circumlocution for it. Nothing in the story acknowledges that a listener might expect one, because acknowledging it is how a fear gets introduced.
Ada does almost nothing when we meet her, on purpose. A beekeeper standing with her sleeves rolled up watching her bees work is the whole safety argument made without a sentence about safety.
s2b was given the shape of the traffic rather than the cargo so that it does not steal the pollen discovery from s2a. It gets one heavy low bee instead, which is a hint rather than the answer.

The two endings each carry both facts, the dance and the legs, because a listener may only ever hear one of them. That is why s4a spends a sentence on a bee unloading her pockets into a cell, and why s4b ends at the hive doorway rather than in the field.

Open question for the psychologist: Barnaby's kind of funny is deadpan, and deadpan depends on hearing the flatness. It should carry in a voice performance and may fall flat read silently by a tired parent.

Craft audit caught both endings over the age 5-6 word ceiling (207 and 209 against 200). Trimmed by cutting restatement rather than story: s4a lost the closing line that repeated in the hero's voice what Ada had just explained, and s4b lost a duplicated description of the dance plus its summary line. Both endings now land on an image instead of a conclusion, which is stronger anyway.
craft_notes: Priming before any threshold, per rule 3: we get the hero and the watered pink flowers by the back door, the garden with two white boxes at the bottom of it, and then the pull arrives at us rather than being sought, a bee passing close enough to move the air past an ear. The first line the hero speaks is the question the story answers.

A character asks both choice questions in their own voice. c1 is Barnaby pointing his nose at two clues, which also gives him a job at the fork instead of a joke. c2 is Ada offering the window or the field. The narrator announces neither.

Similes come only from a five-year-old's own day and are used once each: working a bowl of cereal head down, butter pressed onto a knife, the two escalators at the shops, water going round a stone, the fridge heard at night, the kitchen sounding through the door while everyone in there makes lunch.

One motif, developed rather than replaced: being told. It runs from the hero's question in s1, through the flat two-sentence beat that closes both branches, nobody had told the hero, to Ada's answer in s3, somebody told them, to the thing itself in both endings, that is how they told each other and that is her telling them.

Rhythm alternates deliberately at the beats that matter. s1 puts It did not stop between two long sentences, and breaks the flight line into three fragments, Over the grass, Over the far fence, Gone. s2a lands Rude on its own after a long one. s4b sets Clover alone after the long approach to the gate.

The competence beat is one clause of positioning from Ada, still hands and slow feet and they go round us the way water goes round a stone, followed by a bee landing on a wrist and leaving of its own accord. It gives the beat a vantage point and Ada a job, it happens once per path, and nothing in it says a bee could do anything to anybody.

Description was held to what invites, involves, advances or ignites. The lavender is there because a bee is on it; the bucket is there to be stood on; the humming wood is there to be put an ear against; the clover field is the answer arriving as sound before it arrives as fact.

Barnaby is doing something in every segment rather than standing nearby being funny: he offers the two clues, he sits on a foot to agree, he stands still and holds his breath beside the hive, and in s4b he keeps still under a walking bee, which quietly repeats the competence lesson as comedy instead of instruction.

What I deliberately did not write: no shrinking down and going inside the hive, no bee given a name or a speaking part, no honey-making mechanism piled on top of the dance, no round dance, no veil or smoker, no queen, no swarm, no scolding, no warning of any kind, and no second comic character. The pink flowers are never apologised for either, because they were never the problem.
